name: Feedback Students Actually Use
title: Feedback Students Actually Use
answer: The idea of feedback students actually use is that AI can help teachers give more feedback, but its value depends on whether the feedback is good and whether students act on it. It matters because students often ignore feedback, and because human feedback remains stronger in most categories even when AI is useful for early drafts. The aim is to place AI where it helps and keep teacher judgment for the moments that matter most.

sections.body: AI can increase the amount of feedback a teacher gives, yet quantity alone does not improve writing. The problem is not only generating comments but making them useful enough that students revise. Research in the text shows wide variation in results and a common pattern of students not using feedback. The idea asks teachers to treat feedback as something that must be read, understood and applied, not merely delivered. It also asks schools to think about how feedback is presented, since students may react to who they believe wrote it.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, teachers can use AI for early drafts and save their own detailed comments for later drafts, as the text suggests. For secondary essays, this means AI might support first round comments while the teacher focuses on deeper revision. The text does not give separate routines by grade band, but one study covered students in grades 1 through 12 and found similar rates of ignoring feedback across grades and task types. That suggests the same basic concern applies from elementary through high school. Teachers still need to check whether students change their work after feedback, because feedback that is never used cannot help.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text reports a meta analysis of 20 studies finding a medium sized effect of automated writing feedback on students' writing performance (Fleckenstein et al., 2023), with results varying widely across studies. A study comparing 200 pieces of feedback from trained teachers with 200 from ChatGPT on secondary essays found humans gave higher quality feedback in every category except alignment with criteria (Steiss et al., 2024). Another study found AI and human feedback had similar quality overall, with both weak at helping students think about their own learning (Nazaretsky et al., 2026). In a study of more than 14,000 students in grades 1 through 12, nearly half did not change a single character of their writing after receiving AI feedback, and the rate was about the same across grades and types of tasks (Jansen et al., 2025). The text also reports that students judged feedback by who they believed wrote it, not by its actual quality.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets limits on how far AI feedback should go. Human feedback is still better in most ways, so teachers should not hand over the feedback that matters most. AI may be most useful for early drafts, while teachers keep detailed feedback for later drafts. Students may dismiss good feedback they think came from AI or trust poor feedback they think came from a teacher, so how feedback is presented matters. The decision to use feedback, revise, and judge student work stays with the teacher and student, not with the AI.
